title: The Whistle
notice: An AI-condensed reading. Expand any paragraph for the complete source text.

sections.overview: At seven, I spent all my holiday money on a whistle. My family told me I had paid four times its value and mocked the bargain. Thinking of what else I could have bought left me more upset than the whistle had made me happy.
sections.body: When I was a child at seven years old, my friends on a holiday, filled my pockets with coppers. I went directly to a shop where they sold toys for children ; and being charmed with the sound of a whistle that I met by the way in the hands of another boy, I voluntary offered him all my money for it. I then came home, and went whistling all over the house, much pleased with my whistle, but disturbing all the family. My brothers, and sisters, and cousins, understanding the bargain I had made, told me I had given four times as much for it as it was worth. This put me in mind what good things I might have bought with the rest of the money ; and they laughed at me so much for my folly that I cried with vexation ; and the reflection gave me more chagrin than the whistle gave me pleasure.

sections.overview: That memory later helped me resist unnecessary purchases: I reminded myself not to overpay for another whistle.
sections.body: This, however, was afterwards of use to me, the impression continuing on my mind ; so that often when I was tempted to buy some unnecessary thing, I said to myself, Don't give too much for the whistle ; and so I saved my money.

sections.overview: As I grew older, I thought many people made the same costly mistake.
sections.body: As I grew up, came into the world, and observed the actions of men, I thought I met with many, very many, who gave too much for the whistle.

sections.overview: I saw people sacrifice their time, peace, freedom, virtue, and perhaps their friends for court favour, and judged the price too high.
sections.body: When I saw any one too ambitious of court favours, sacrificing his time in attendance or levees, his repose, his liberty, his virtue, and perhaps his friends, to attain it, I have said to myself, This man gives too much for his whistle.

sections.overview: When the pursuit of popularity ruined a person’s own affairs, I thought the recognition cost too much.
sections.body: When I saw another fond of popularity, constantly employing himself in political bustles, neglecting his own affairs, and ruining them by that neglect: He pays, indeed, says I, too much for his whistle.

sections.overview: I thought a miser paid too dearly for wealth when it cost comfort, generosity, others’ esteem, and friendship.
sections.body: If I knew a miser, who gave up every kind of comfortable living, all the pleasure of doing good to others, all the esteem of his fellow- citizens, and the joys of benevolent friendship, for the sake of accumulating wealth: Poor man, says I, you do indeed pay too much for your whistle.

sections.overview: When bodily pleasure displaced every worthwhile improvement of mind or fortune, I thought it bought pain instead.
sections.body: When I meet a man of pleasure, sacrificing every laudable improvement of the mind, or of his fortune to mere corporeal sensations ; Mistaken man, says I, you are providing pain for yourself instead of pleasure ; you give too much for your whistle.

sections.overview: When appearances drove someone beyond their means into debt and prison, I thought the price ruinously high.
sections.body: If I see one fond of fine clothes, fine furniture, fine equipages, all above his fortune, for which he contracts debts, and ends his career in prison: Alas ! says I, he has paid dear, very dear for his whistle.

sections.overview: I pitied a kind young woman whose marriage to an ill-natured husband seemed another costly bargain.
sections.body: When I see a beautiful sweet tempered girl married to an ill-natured husband: What a pity it is, says I, that she has paid so much for a whistle!

sections.overview: I came to believe that much human misery comes from misjudging what things are worth and paying too much for them.
sections.body: In short, I conceived that great part of the miseries of mankind were brought upon them by the false estimates they had made of the value of things, and by their giving too much for their whistle.
